case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: J.P.H. v. Florida Department of Children & Families
key_cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District
key_cases.holding: Termination of parental rights to Indian children was reversed because the trial court applied Florida's clear-and-convincing standard instead of ICWA's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard and wrongly denied the tribe intervention for lack of Florida counsel.
key_cases.relevance: J.P.H. is the clearest Florida holding that ICWA displaces Chapter 39's proof standard and guarantees the tribe's right to intervene.
key_cases.quote: which requires that any order terminating parental rights to an Indian child be supported "by evidence beyond a reasonable doubt," rather than the clear and convincing evidence standard

key_cases.case_name: Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Department of Children & Families
key_cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Fourth District
key_cases.holding: A trial court's finding of good cause to deviate from ICWA's placement preferences is reviewed for abuse of discretion, and the deviation was affirmed where the record showed the court understood the statutory scheme and found the tribal family could not presently meet the child's needs.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Florida decision applying ICWA's placement-preference scheme once a tribe intervenes in a state dependency case.
key_cases.quote: choosing to apply Florida's abuse of discretion standard to the review of a trial court's finding of good cause to deviate

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: 'Domicile' in ICWA section 1911(a) is defined by uniform federal law, not state law; twins born off-reservation to parents domiciled on the Choctaw reservation were themselves domiciled there, so the tribal court had exclusive jurisdiction and the state adoption decree was reversed.
key_cases.relevance: Holyfield is the Supreme Court's foundational ICWA decision and the starting point for any Florida jurisdictional analysis involving an Indian child, including the threshold question of exclusive tribal jurisdiction.
key_cases.quote: These congressional objectives make clear that a rule of domicile that would permit individual Indian parents to defeat the ICWA's jurisdictional scheme is inconsistent with what Congress intended

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: ICWA section 1912(f)'s beyond-a-reasonable-doubt 'continued custody' requirement does not apply to a parent who never had custody, section 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family, and section 1915(a)'s preferences do not bar a non-Indian adoption when no preferred party has sought to adopt.
key_cases.relevance: Adoptive Couple directly qualifies the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt proposition Florida's J.P.H. draws from section 1912(f), so INP-11 overstates that holding without it.
key_cases.quote: §1912(f) does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody of the Indian child.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court upheld Congress's Article I authority to enact ICWA and rejected the anticommandeering challenges on the merits, while vacating the equal protection and nondelegation rulings because no petitioner had standing to press them.
key_cases.relevance: Brackeen is the current baseline for ICWA's constitutional validity and binding force on Florida state courts, and it is the authority a 2026-dated brief must cite alongside the older Florida DCA decisions.
key_cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(a)
Physicians, osteopathic physicians, medical examiners, chiropractic physicians, nurses, and hospital personnel — must give their name when reporting, Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(b)2.a.
Health care professionals and mental health professionals — must give their name when reporting, Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(b)2.b.
Practitioners who rely solely on spiritual means for healing — must give their name when reporting, Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(b)2.c.
School teachers and other school officials or personnel — must give their name when reporting, Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(b)2.d.
Social workers, day care center workers, and other professional child care, foster care, residential, or institutional workers — must give their name when reporting, Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(b)2.e.
Law enforcement officers — must give their name when reporting, Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(b)2.f.
Judges — must give their name when reporting, Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(b)2.g.
Animal control officers — must give their name when reporting, Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(b)2.h.
reporting_details: In Florida any person who knows, or has reasonable cause to suspect, that a child is abused, abandoned, or neglected must report it immediately to the statewide central abuse hotline (Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(a)); members of the general public may report anonymously, but reporters in the professions listed in Fla. Stat. § 39.201(1)(b)2. must give their names.

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediate response, or 24-hour response; an immediate response may be downgraded to a 24-hour response only on information obtained after the Florida Abuse Hotline screening showing that the child is no longer in imminent danger of being harmed
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Report received by the Florida Abuse Hotline
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Fla. Admin. Code R. 65C-29.003
